about: Every departure from the server guide that the Brennan's pack makes, each with its reason and its source, so a reader can audit the pack against the guide (house/brennans/guide.txt, menus read 26 September 2026) and the research under house/brennans/research/. The builder (house/build-brennans.mjs) applies the entries in order after parsing and before dash stripping; a replace whose 'from' is not found fails the build. Verdict ids (chef-dishes-b-4, gap-pron-6 and so on) are the ids in research/verified-facts.json; 'pdf-corrections pN' points at research/pdf-corrections.json by page. A still-unverifiable fact is placed nowhere as a fact; a refuted claim appears only as its correction. A price is never touched here, except where a newer printed menu prints another: from the 01:30 edition of 4 October 2026 the owner's paste of 3 October sets the Damien Martin and the Durban glass prices, each with the older figure kept as a dispute. Targets: house | dish:<name> | wine:<name> | cocktail:<name> | tasting:<name> | term:<term> | scenario:<title> | mixup:<a> vs <b> | mustknow:<title> | <list>:+ to add. Ops: set (default), replace {from,to}, append, add, retire {tombstone}. A retire takes a dish, wine or drink the current menus no longer print out of the house and puts its id in house.removed under the stamp named, a millisecond after the last edition that carried it, so a device drops the copy nobody touched; an add on wine:+ files a whole wine, and an add on house sources files a source. From the 3 October 2026 edition, an add on dish:+ or cocktail:+ files a whole item the guide prints only as a price line or a must-know, or a house page the research read prints (the 1946 list, the Luxury Roost Bar cocktails, the premium Sazeracs, the eye openers, the coffees and juice, the children's menu, the Bubbles snacks); every such price stands verbatim on guide.txt or on a snapshot under house/brennans/pages/ whose first line names its source. From the 22:00 edition of 3 October 2026, every dish, drink and wine also carries an add on kept for each fixed question of docs/study-menus-design.md section 5 (Tell me about it., How do I sell it?, What do guests ask?, What should I watch for?, and How do I pour it? for every wine and the drinks finished at the table), each with a reason opening Study notes and its sources, and every thin guest line (engine.mjs thinLines) is rewritten by a set whose reason opens Thin line with its code; engine.mjs noteProblems holds both in validate-pack, keep-all and check-pack. From the 01:30 edition of 4 October 2026 an add on dispute:+ may carry a resolution, which says which side a newer printed menu bears out while both sides stay, and a mix-up is named mixup:<a> vs <b> by its two sides.

principles.reason: The guide prints five pairing principles outside the engine's nine. In the guide's own formula (p3) bubbles sit under Fat (butter and fried food want acidity or bubbles), umami under Salt & umami, and smoke is listed under Bridge (a shared flavour: herbs, citrus, smoke, mushroom, butter, toast), so each maps there when the block does not already carry that principle; temp and texture have no home among the nine and are dropped. The builder logs every change in its report.

entries.value: Owen Brennan opened the restaurant on Bourbon Street in July 1946, and it has been at 417 Royal Street since 1956. Owen died in November 1955, before the move; Ella Brennan found the backing and the family opened Royal Street in 1956. The building dates from 1795, was the first bank in Louisiana and later the home of Paul Morphy, the chess champion; the bank's initials survive in the balcony ironwork. The family split in November 1973, settled in 1974: Owen's widow Maude and sons Pip, Jimmy and Ted kept Royal Street, and Ella's side took Commander's Palace. Brennan's closed in June 2013 and reopened in November 2014 under Ralph Brennan and Terry White after a restoration of the whole house. Paul Blange, the first chef, created Bananas Foster and Eggs Hussarde; Michael Roussel, Lazone Randolph, Slade Rushing and Ryan Hacker followed him, and Kris Padalino has led the kitchen since June 2025. 2026 is the 80th year.
entries.reason: The history the guide omits: Owen's death in 1955, the 2013 closure and the November 2014 reopening under Ralph Brennan and Terry White, the building of 1795 and Paul Morphy, the family split, the chef lineage

entries.value: Invented here in 1951, when Owen Brennan asked his sister Ella and chef Paul Blange for a banana dessert, and named for his friend Richard Foster, chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission (also called the Metropolitan Crime Commission). New Orleans was then the main port for bananas from Central America. Butter, light brown sugar and cinnamon, banana liqueur, then the bananas, then aged rum set alight at the table, over housemade vanilla ice cream.

entries.value: Eggs Sardou was created at Antoine's, usually dated 1908, for the French playwright Victorien Sardou. The original was poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, anchovy, ham and truffle, with no spinach. The creamed spinach most kitchens use now came later. Ours fries the artichokes, makes the spinach with Parmesan and swaps hollandaise for Choron, a bearnaise with tomato.

entries.value: Debris, DAY-bree, is the New Orleans word for the shreds of slow cooked meat that fall into their own gravy. Mother's on Poydras Street, open since 1938, made the word famous: its story is that founder Simon Landry asked a customer whether he wanted some of the debris from the roast beef carving board. Ours is short rib braised in red wine until it falls apart.

entries.value: Grand Isle Jewels are farmed oysters from Grand Isle on the Louisiana coast, raised in floating cages above the seabed and tumbled so they grow a deep cup and a clean shell. The brand brought the island's farmers together in 2025 and honors the late Jules Melancon, the first permitted to farm off bottom in 2012; the menu's singular Jewel is the plural brand Jewels. Clean, briny and cold, served raw with a preserved Fresno chili mignonette.

value.q: Personality or Oh! What It Seemed to Be with the raw oysters?
value.a: Offer the Personality, a zero-proof sparkling rosé with tart cherry: the mignonette already supplies acid and the Personality supplies the one thing the plate lacks, bubbles. A server may offer the Oh! What It Seemed to Be to a guest who wants lemon and agave with the mignonette. Test both at lineup. Fresno is a red Californian chili from the 1950s, about the heat of a jalapeno but fruitier and thinner walled; preserved and stirred into the mignonette it gives a gentle warmth, not real heat.

value.q: What is the classic Sazerac build, and is it ours?
value.a: The Classic Sazerac at Brennan's is Sazerac rye stirred with Peychaud's bitters, served without ice in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint (ERB-saint), $13; confirm sugar and lemon peel with the bar. The Sazerac Company's own recipe is a sugar cube, three dashes of Peychaud's, an ounce and a half of Sazerac Rye, a quarter ounce of Herbsaint and a lemon peel, built across two glasses and served neat in a chilled rocks glass; the IBA version is Cognac based with absinthe. Give those as the classic, never as the house build. If a guest asks for it on the rocks, check with the bar before promising it. Two luxury versions: Thompson's Dream with Willett rye, and Origin Story with Cognac and absinthe; the price ladder is $13, $20 and $40.

value.q: The cellar dossier's second opinion on the pairing?

value.title: Creole versus Cajun
value.guest: What’s the difference between Creole and Cajun?
value.you: Creole is New Orleans city cooking: French and Spanish at the root, African and Caribbean hands in it, more butter, cream and tomato, more sauces. Cajun is the country cooking of Acadiana, from the Acadian exiles, one pot, dark roux, rustic and spicier. Brennan’s is Creole. You’ll hear me say Cajun for a few ingredients, like the tasso in the shrimp and grits.
value.principle: Two sentences, then back to the menu.

value.title: The chefs
value.body: Paul Blangé, the chef behind Bananas Foster, led the kitchen until the 1970s. Michael Roussel, who started here in 1956 and trained under Blangé, became executive chef in 1974 and retired in 2005 after 49 years. Lazone Randolph, who began as a dishwasher in 1965, succeeded him in 2005 and gave his name to Chicken Lazone. Slade Rushing ran the kitchen from the 2014 reopening to 2019 and Ryan Hacker from late 2019 to spring 2025. Our executive chef is Kris Padalino, who took over in June 2025 after eight years in this kitchen as pastry chef and executive sous chef; she trained at Le Cordon Bleu in Pasadena and cooked in Los Angeles and Denver before New Orleans.

entries.source: chef-history-15; chef-dishes-a-23; pdf-factcheck-4

value.title: The building and the family
value.body: 1795: it was Louisiana's first bank, then the home of Paul Morphy, the chess champion; look for the bank's initials in the balcony ironwork. Owen Brennan opened on Bourbon Street in July 1946 and the house moved here in 1956, after Owen's death in November 1955, with Ella Brennan finding the backing. The family split in November 1973, settled in 1974: Owen's side kept Royal Street, Ella's side took Commander's Palace; Brennan's of Houston belongs to Ella's side, so a guest who ate at Brennan's in Houston ate at a cousin. The house closed on 28 June 2013 and reopened on 25 November 2014 under Ralph Brennan and Terry White after seventeen months of restoration.

value.title: The courtyard turtles

Their return to the fountain in 2015 began the annual Slowest Second Line on Earth. Say it before the guest asks: the turtle soup is not the turtles.

lines.s10: The Yellowstone: Uncle Nearest whiskey with Peychaud's Aperitivo, our honey and turmeric syrup, and lemon.
lines.s20: From our Summer Vacations of 1946 list, the Yellowstone is Uncle Nearest 1884 whiskey with lemon, our housemade honey and turmeric syrup and Peychaud's Aperitivo: honeyed, bright and a little bittersweet.
lines.s45: Our cocktail list is themed Summer Vacations of 1946, the year Brennan's opened, and the Yellowstone is the national park trip. It's Uncle Nearest 1884, a small batch whiskey, with fresh lemon, a honey and turmeric syrup we make here, and Peychaud's Aperitivo, a bittersweet red aperitif under the same New Orleans name as our Sazerac bitters. Honey and lemon make it easy to drink, and the aperitivo gives it a grown-up edge. If you like a whiskey sour, you'll like this.

value.guest: Uncle Nearest whiskey with honey, turmeric, lemon and Peychaud's Aperitivo: honeyed, bright and a little bittersweet.
value.why: Sell it to the whiskey sour drinker and to anyone who wants something lighter than a Sazerac; at $18.00 it is the top of the 1946 list.

lines.s10: The Miami Beach: sparkling wine with local watermelon juice and fresh citrus. Light and summery.
lines.s20: The Miami Beach is the lightest drink on our 1946 list: sparkling wine with local watermelon juice and fresh citrus. Fizzy, fruity and gentler than a spirit cocktail, it is a lovely brunch or courtyard drink.
lines.s45: If you'd like something light, the Miami Beach is the beach stop on our Summer Vacations of 1946 list. It's sparkling wine with local watermelon juice and fresh citrus, so it's fizzy, fruity and gentle, lighter than a spirit cocktail. It's a natural at brunch or out in the courtyard. If you'd love the same idea without alcohol, our Catalina Island is watermelon and tonic, and to go grander after your meal, come up to the Roost Bar for the Flamingo, made with Taittinger Champagne.

value.why: The easy yes at brunch and in the courtyard, and the lowest price on the 1946 list at $14.00; the sparkling twin of the Catalina Island.

lines.s10: The Niagara Falls: gin, Lillet Blanc, tomato water and lemon. Crisp, savory and refreshing.
lines.s20: The Niagara Falls is gin with Lillet Blanc, a light French aperitif wine, plus tomato water and lemon: crisp and savory, like the freshest part of a ripe tomato, with a soft floral note.
lines.s45: The Niagara Falls is the gin drink on our 1946 list. It's gin with Lillet Blanc, a light French aperitif wine, then tomato water, the clear juice of ripe tomatoes, and fresh lemon. So it tastes crisp and savory rather than sweet, with a gentle floral, citrusy lift from the Lillet. It's lovely before a meal and with oysters or the Creole tomato tostada. If you like a martini but want something lighter, this is the one. After your meal, our Roost Bar pours the Spoonbill, the grand gin drink.

value.guest: Gin with Lillet Blanc, tomato water and lemon: crisp, savory and refreshing.
value.why: The savory, not sweet, drink on the list: offer it to a martini or gin drinker and before oysters.

lines.s45: The Havana is the island stop on our 1946 list. It's built on Appleton Estate 12 Year Old, an aged rum with plenty of brown sugar and oak, with more brown sugar syrup, fresh lime and spicy ginger beer, so it drinks like a richer rum and ginger. value.s10: The Pierre Sparr: a sparkling rosé from Alsace, all Pinot Noir, dry with bright berry fruit.
value.s20: If you'd like something pink and festive, the Pierre Sparr is a Crémant d'Alsace rosé, made like Champagne from all Pinot Noir: strawberry and red currant, dry, with a creamy mousse, at a friendlier price.
value.s45: The Pierre Sparr is a Crémant d'Alsace rosé. Crémant means it's made the same way as Champagne, with the second fermentation in the bottle, and in Alsace a rosé crémant must be all Pinot Noir. So you get strawberry and red currant, dry, with a creamy mousse, at a friendlier price than Champagne. The red fruit and bubbles make it our first pick with the steak tartare cannoli, and it's lovely with the fried hen, the Sardou and the Owen, or a brunch celebration.

value.a:
The Baked Apple is the first plated course of the Traditional Breakfast at Brennan's, our $80 tasting, and it is served only on that menu.

A whole apple is peeled, cored and baked until soft under a crumble of rolled oats, pecans, raisins, brown sugar and cinnamon, then glazed with brown sugar. It goes out with sweetened crème fraîche, a slightly tangy cultured cream, beside it.

What the guest gets is a warm, soft apple under its crumble and glaze, with the cool cream alongside. It eats like a warm apple crisp: tender fruit, a little crunch, cinnamon sweetness, and the tang of the cream to balance it.

Breakfast here has always been a long, celebratory meal, and this is its gentle start. It follows the Brandy Milk Punch eye opener and comes before the soup. The tasting includes its drinks, so wine is only ever an extra here; for a guest who wants one, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle tastes of baked apple and honey and carries on to the Bananas Foster.

If a guest wants wine beyond the included drinks, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle at $80 is the match and lasts to dessert. Say: “The tasting starts sweet and gentle: a warm baked apple with an oat and pecan crumble, like an apple crisp.”

value.a:
The Petite Filet Mignon is the fourth course of the Traditional Breakfast, the last savory course before the Bananas Foster, and the steak a grand New Orleans breakfast has always included.

It is a small filet mignon, the most tender cut of beef, cooked to the temperature the guest chose when the tasting was ordered. Beside it sit a potato rösti, RUHSH-tee, a Swiss-style cake of shredded potato fried golden and crisp, and garlicky wilted spinach.

The plate is simple on purpose: the beef, the crisp potato cake and the green spinach. It tastes tender, beefy and clean, with crunch from the rösti and garlic from the spinach.

The course comes with a 4 oz glass of Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’, a Côtes du Rhône from old vine Syrah grown beside Châteauneuf-du-Pape: black raspberry, pepper and soft tannins, juicy enough for red meat and light enough for the morning. The pour is included in the $80 price.

The Louisiana BBQ Lobster is the second course of our $80 dinner tasting, between the Grand Isle Jewel oysters and the Redfish Véronique.

New Orleans barbecue is not a smoker or a tomato sauce. It is the buttery, peppery style made famous by barbecue shrimp, and here the kitchen gives that treatment to lobster. The lobster sits on a white bean stew with ’nduja, en-DOO-yah, a soft, spreadable, spicy pork sausage from Calabria in southern Italy that melts into the beans.

The guest gets sweet lobster over a creamy stew of beans warmed by the sausage. It tastes sweet and rich from the lobster and the butter, with a warm red-pepper heat and a smoky, creamy base.

It is the course that brings spice into the tasting. On the $120 wine pairing it is poured with a 4 oz glass of white Burgundy, the Fichet ‘Château London’ Mâcon-Igé 2024 on the guide's card: Chardonnay round enough for the butter and fresh enough for the ’nduja.

The Roasted Rohan Duck Breast is the fourth course of our $80 dinner tasting, the last savory course before The Snickers.

Rohan, ROH-han, is a special cross bred for the D'Artagnan company and raised in New York's Hudson Valley for tender, rosy meat. The breast is roasted so the skin renders and the meat stays rosy. On the late summer card it comes with peaches glazed in cane syrup, Louisiana's own sugarcane syrup, lighter and more buttery than molasses, and candied hazelnuts.

The guest gets slices of rosy duck with caramel-glazed fruit and a little crunch from the nuts. It tastes rich and savory against the sweet fruit.

Duck and fruit is a French classic, and this is the Louisiana version. On the $120 pairing it is poured with a 4 oz glass of Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon 2021, dark fruit for the peaches and structure for the duck.

The plate has changed on the house page since the guide was read, so the garnish is confirmed with the kitchen every night.

The Blackberry Trifle is one of the three sweet starters on our breakfast and lunch menu, at $14, and a lighter way to begin the meal.

A trifle is a layered dessert. Ours layers blackberry curd and lemon curd with coconut chia pudding, chia seeds soaked until they turn soft and spoonable, and finishes with blackberry financier biscuits, fee-nahn-SYAY, small, buttery French cakes, traditionally made with almond flour, that give it texture; what is in ours is a question for the kitchen and the service note.

What arrives is a layered sweet of two curds, the pudding and the little cakes. It tastes bright, tart and creamy, fruity more than sugary, so it wakes the palate up rather than weighing it down.

It is made to share: it belongs in the middle of the table while the guests look over the egg dishes. If the table wants wine with its sweet starters, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle is the match, honeyed and racy enough for the curds, and it lasts through to dessert. Without alcohol, the Personality, a zero-proof sparkling rosé, keeps it light.

The Framboise French Toast is a sweet starter on our breakfast and lunch menu at $16, made to share or to enjoy as a sweet course.

Framboise, frahm-BWAHZ, is French for raspberry, and raspberry is the star. We bake our own citrus brioche, a rich, buttery egg bread, and turn it into French toast. It is finished with mascarpone mousse, a rich Italian cream cheese whipped light, a raspberry coulis, which is a smooth fruit sauce, and fresh local raspberries on top.

The guest gets French toast under the mousse, the red coulis and whole berries. It tastes rich, soft and custardy, with bright, tart berry against the cream and a little citrus from the brioche.

Baking the brioche in house is what sets it apart. With it, the Dr. Hermann Auslese half-bottle keeps the raspberries juicy, and our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory balances the sweetness for a guest who wants no wine.

The Café Brûlot Coffee Cake is a sweet starter on our breakfast and lunch menu at $14. It is named for café brûlot, ka-FAY broo-LOH, the classic New Orleans coffee flamed with brandy, orange and lemon peel, cinnamon and clove.

The cake borrows those flavors. It is a chicory coffee and bittersweet chocolate cake with pecans for crunch, finished with a spiced citrus glaze and whipped crème fraîche, a slightly tangy cultured cream that keeps it from being too sweet.

The guest gets a dark, moist cake with its glaze and a spoon of the cream. It tastes roasty and chocolatey, with orange and warm spice.

Café brûlot itself is on no current menu as a drink: this cake is the only Brûlot item, and only two desserts are flamed at the table. The natural partner is a cup of our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory. For wine, Banyuls, a sweet red from the south of France, carries its own cocoa and coffee notes, once the sommelier confirms it can be poured at breakfast.

The Louisiana Oysters are a starter on our breakfast and lunch menu at $19, and the oyster dish of the daytime menu.

In New Orleans, barbecue does not mean a smoker or a tomato sauce. It means the style made famous by barbecue shrimp: a rich, buttery sauce with plenty of black pepper. The kitchen serves Louisiana oysters in that sauce, then adds pickled collard greens for a sharp, bright bite, shallots, and a fried saltine crumble for crunch.

The guest gets oysters in a peppery butter sauce, with the bright greens and a crunchy crumble. It tastes rich and peppery, with a sharp pickled bite: peppery, not hot.

It is a dish to share before the eggs, and a real New Orleans flavor. The guide pours the Gainey Estate Chardonnay with it, creamy enough for the butter sauce and fresh enough for the pickled greens; for a guest who wants bubbles cutting the butter, the house Champagne is the second choice.

The Creole Tomato Tostada is a dinner starter at $18, and our celebration of Louisiana tomato season.

Creole tomatoes are Louisiana's summer tomato: juicy, sweet and a little tart. Here they are mixed with heirloom tomatoes and served raw and simply, with creamy burrata, boo-RAH-tah, fresh mozzarella with a soft, creamy center. They sit on a crisp tostada, a flat shell the kitchen makes in house with okra, and a smoked tomato water, a clear, intensely tomatoey broth, is poured around.

The guest sees bright tomatoes and white burrata on the crisp shell, with the clear broth around them. It tastes juicy, sweet and tart, cool and creamy, with crunch and a whisper of smoke.

It is light, seasonal and gone when the tomatoes are, so it changes as the season turns. The Minuty rosé from Provence is the pour, dry and bright enough for raw tomato and delicate enough for the burrata.

The Louisiana Crab Claws are a dinner starter at $22, a Louisiana favorite and a dish to share.

Crab claws are sweet, delicate crab meat you eat straight off the claw, using the pincer as a handle. Ours come warm, dressed in a brown butter vinaigrette: butter cooked until it turns nutty and toasty, balanced with acidity so it is rich but bright. Fines herbes, feen ZAIRB, the classic French mix of parsley, chives, tarragon and chervil, finish it with a soft, fresh green note.

The guest gets warm claws glossed in the vinaigrette under green herbs, with a plate for the shells and napkins brought at the same time. It tastes of sweet crab, nutty butter, bright acid and soft herbs.

It is simple and elegant. The guide pours the Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin with it, because white Burgundy's nutty richness mirrors the brown butter; the sommelier may suggest the Gainey Chardonnay as a lower priced, creamy option once it is confirmed to taste fresh.

The Grand Isle Jewel Oysters are a dinner starter at $22, and the first course of our $80 dinner tasting.

Grand Isle is a barrier island on Louisiana's coast. Grand Isle Jewels are farmed oysters raised there in floating cages above the seabed and tumbled, so they grow a deep cup and a clean shell. The brand brought the island's farmers together in 2025 and honors the late Jules Melancon, the first permitted to farm off bottom there, in 2012. We serve them raw on the half shell with a mignonette, meen-yo-NET, the classic raw bar sauce of vinegar, shallot and cracked pepper, made here with preserved Fresno chili, and parsley.

The guest gets cold oysters on the shell with the mignonette and a green note of parsley. They taste clean, briny and cold, the vinegar bright and the chili a gentle warmth, not real heat.

Oysters and Champagne are the classic: the house Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut is the pour à la carte, and the dinner tasting pours Charles Lafitte Brut.

The Steak Tartare Cannoli is a dinner starter at $17, a playful take on steak tartare.

Tartare is raw beef, finely chopped and seasoned. Instead of serving it with toast, the kitchen pipes it into a crisp potato shell shaped like a cannoli. Crème fraîche, krem FRESH, a tangy cultured cream, keeps it cool and silky, and an egg yolk cured until firm is grated over the top the way Italians grate bottarga, boh-TAR-gah, the cured fish roe, for a rich, salty finish.

The guest gets a handheld piece, two or three bites, crisp outside and cool within. It tastes cool, silky and savory, the shell crunching against the soft beef and the salty yolk.

It is the only dish on the current menus with the cured egg yolk, and a fun way to start dinner. The Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d'Alsace is the pour: all Pinot Noir, with red fruit for the raw beef and bubbles for the fried shell and the cream.

value.a:
Turtle Soup is a Brennan's signature, $13 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and the soup on the Traditional Breakfast.

It is one of the great Creole soups, rich and long-cooked. Ours is made with 100% turtle meat, farm raised Louisiana freshwater turtle, never wild. Many New Orleans turtle soups stretch the turtle with veal and beef; ours is all turtle, with nothing padding it out. It is finished with brown butter spinach, grated egg and a splash of aged Sherry at the end.

The guest gets a deep, dark bowl with the spinach and egg through it. It tastes savory and meaty, with a toasty, earthy note from the brown butter spinach, richness from the egg, and a nutty, dry lift from the Sherry that cuts the richness. If they have never had turtle, it is like a rich, finely chopped stew.

It is the one bowl that tells a guest what Brennan's is about. Our house Champagne, very dry, cleans the palate between spoonfuls and picks up the Sherry.

The Seafood Gumbo is a Brennan's signature, $13 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and the other soup choice on the Traditional Breakfast.

Gumbo, GUM-boh, is the dish that says Louisiana: a stew built on a dark roux. Ours is all about the seafood, shrimp, crab and oysters, so every spoonful has sweetness and a little brine. Andouille, ahn-DOO-ee, a coarse, smoked pork sausage, gives it a savory, smoky backbone and a gentle warmth. It is served over popcorn rice, a Louisiana long-grain with a nutty, toasty aroma that really does smell a little like popcorn.

The guest gets a hearty bowl of seafood and sausage over the rice. It tastes savory, briny and smoky, with mild to moderate spice.

Our published gumbo recipe starts with a dark mahogany roux, and the seafood goes in at the very end so it stays tender; whether the dining room follows it is confirmed at lineup. The Berres Riesling is the pour: light and bright, it cools the spice and keeps the seafood sweet.

value.a:
The Creole Caesar is our salad, $15 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and our Louisiana take on a Caesar.

It starts with gem lettuce, small, sweet and very crisp, so it holds up to a creamy dressing. The dressing is made with smoked oysters, which give it the deep, savory flavor a Caesar is known for, with a smoky edge. Grana Padano, GRAH-nah pah-DAH-noh, a hard, nutty Italian cheese like Parmesan, adds salt and richness, and the crisps are made from Leidenheimer, LY-den-hy-mer, the bakery behind New Orleans' po-boy bread since 1896.

The guest gets crisp leaves in a creamy dressing with shaved cheese and crunchy bread crisps. It tastes crisp, creamy, smoky and savory.

It is a lighter start before an egg dish or the redfish, and it appears at both meals. The Pazo das Bruxas Albariño is the pour: citrusy, with a salty, coastal edge that meets the smoked oyster dressing.

value.a:
Eggs Hussarde, hoo-SARD, is our signature egg dish, $27 at breakfast and lunch, and the heart of the Traditional Breakfast.

It is the New Orleans cousin of Eggs Benedict. We make our own English muffins, and the Canadian bacon is cured with coffee, so it is smoky and a little roasty. On top go poached eggs and two sauces: hollandaise, the buttery, lemony egg-yolk sauce, and marchand de vin, mar-SHAHN duh VAN, the wine merchant's sauce, a savory red wine and mushroom sauce.

The guest gets the eggs on their muffins and bacon, the two sauces side by side. It tastes rich, buttery and savory, with a deep, winey note and a bright, lemony edge.

Paul Blangé, the house's first chef, is credited with creating it, alongside Bananas Foster and Chicken Pontalba; confirm the house's wording before telling that story. Eggs and Champagne are made for each other: our house Piper-Heidsieck is very dry, so it keeps the hollandaise feeling light.

value.a:
Eggs Sardou, sar-DOO, is one of the classic New Orleans egg dishes, a Brennan's signature at $26 on the breakfast and lunch menu.

It was created at Antoine's, usually dated 1908, for the French playwright Victorien Sardou. The original set poached eggs on artichoke bottoms with hollandaise, anchovy, ham and truffle, with no spinach; the creamed spinach most kitchens use came later. Ours fries the artichokes until crisp, makes the creamed spinach with Parmesan, and swaps the hollandaise for Choron, sho-ROHN, a béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, with tomato folded in.

The guest gets poached eggs over the crispy artichokes and creamy spinach, finished with the Choron. It tastes creamy and rich, with crunch, and the tomato and tarragon keep it tangy and herbal.

It is our version of a classic born down the street, never a Brennan's invention. Artichokes are hard on most wines, and a crisp Loire Sauvignon Blanc is the exception, so the Durand is the pour.

value.a:
Eggs Owen is our heartiest egg dish, $32 on the breakfast and lunch menu, and steak and eggs, New Orleans style.

It is built on short rib débris. Débris, DAY-bree, is the New Orleans word for slow-cooked meat that falls apart into its own gravy; Mother's on Poydras Street, open since 1938, made the word famous. Ours is short rib braised in red wine until it falls apart. It sits with a Creole-spiced potato and a soft-boiled egg, so the yolk runs into everything, and it takes the same two sauces as the Hussarde: hollandaise for richness, and marchand de vin, a savory red wine and mushroom sauce that doubles down on the braise.

The guest gets a generous plate of tender beef, potato and egg under the two sauces. It tastes meaty, rich and saucy, with mild spice and silky yolk.

Both sauces carry red wine, so a red makes sense: the Domaine de Durban from the Southern Rhône is ripe and generous, with soft tannins gentle enough for the eggs.

The Duck Confit Waffle is a breakfast and lunch entrée at $32, chicken and waffles gone luxurious.

The duck is a Rohan duck leg made as confit, kohn-FEE: cured and cooked slowly in its own fat until it is tender, with crisp skin. It sits on a savory cornbread and chive waffle, and foie gras butter melts in for extra richness. Mustard maple syrup brings sweetness with a little tang to balance it, and a sunny-side-up egg ties it together.

The guest gets the crisp duck leg on the golden waffle, the egg on top and the syrup beside it. It tastes crisp, rich and savory-sweet, the maple and mustard cutting the duck and the butter.

It is a showstopper for a brunch guest who wants something different. The Berres Riesling is the pour: off-dry, its ripe fruit keeps pace with the maple while its acidity cuts the confit fat and the foie gras butter.

New Orleans Shrimp & Grits is a breakfast and lunch entrée at $25, our take on the Southern classic, with a twist.

Instead of a bowl of grits, the grits are made with pimento cheese, set into a cake and fried, so they are crisp outside and creamy inside. Louisiana shrimp go on top in a Creole sauce, a tomato-based sauce with the holy trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper, seasoned with tasso, TAH-so, a smoky, spiced Cajun ham. Fried okra chips go on top for crunch.

The guest gets the golden grit cake under the shrimp and their red sauce, with the okra chips over it all. It tastes creamy and crisp, smoky and tangy, with mild to moderate spice.

It is one of the best values on the menu, and a dish that feels very New Orleans at midday. The Minuty rosé from Provence is the pour: dry and refreshing, bright enough for the tomato and fruity enough for the tasso.

value.a:
The Pecan Gulf Fish is a breakfast and lunch entrée at $31, our Gulf fish plate, and lighter than the egg dishes.

The fish changes with what is fresh, so the server learns today's catch at lineup. It is topped with Louisiana lump crab, the sweet, meaty pieces from the body of the crab, and sauced with a pecan bordelaise, nutty and savory. In New Orleans, bordelaise often means garlic butter rather than the classic French red wine sauce, and the kitchen confirms which it is. Underneath sit a silky cauliflower purée and wilted collard greens.

The guest gets the fish crowned with crab over the pale purée and dark greens, with the pecan sauce. It tastes nutty, buttery and sweet from the crab, with earthy greens.

It is satisfying without being heavy. The Gainey Estate Chardonnay is the pour, creamy enough for the pecans and crab and fresh enough for the fish; if tonight's bordelaise is red-wine based, the Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir takes its place.

The Crab & Corn Omelette is a breakfast and lunch entrée at $28, a summer-in-Louisiana omelette and a lighter choice that still feels special.

It is filled with Louisiana lump crab and roasted sweet corn, both naturally sweet, so they suit each other. Our house-made miso butter adds a savory, almost nutty depth, and lemon and basil keep it fresh. On top goes a gremolata, greh-moh-LAH-tah, a bright Italian mix of herbs and citrus zest, made here with Marcona almonds, the rich, tender Spanish almonds, for crunch.

The guest gets a folded omelette with the butter, the herbs and the crunchy topping. It tastes sweet, buttery and savory, with a bright herbal crunch.

It is the egg dish for a guest who does not want hollandaise. The guide pours the Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin with it, white Burgundy rich enough for the crab and butter and bright enough for the lemon; the Gainey Chardonnay is worth offering too, once the sommelier confirms it tastes fresh.

The Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak is a breakfast and lunch entrée at $38, steak and eggs done properly.

Hanger is a butcher's favorite cut, loose-grained and very beefy, and ours is USDA Prime from Creekstone Farms, a Kansas producer of Black Angus beef, seasoned with Creole spice. It comes with a smoked potato pavé, pah-VAY, thin potato slices layered, pressed, cut into a neat block and crisped, a sunny-side-up egg from Vital Farms, whose hens are pasture raised, and classic French béarnaise, bair-NAYZ: butter, egg yolk, shallot and tarragon.

The guest gets the sliced steak beside the crisp potato block, the egg with its runny yolk and the béarnaise. It tastes beefy and spiced, with a smoky, crisp potato and a rich sauce.

It is at its best medium-rare to medium. The Moulin d'Issan Bordeaux Supérieur is the pour: a classic Bordeaux with cassis and cedar and the structure for beef and béarnaise, not too heavy for midday.

The Roasted Chateaubriand is our dinner centerpiece for two, $120, and a celebration dish.

Chateaubriand, shah-toh-bree-AHN, is the classic French cut for two: the thickest, most tender center of the beef tenderloin. Ours is Creekstone Farms beef, roasted whole so it stays juicy. It comes with roasted and glazed summer squash and sauce Foyot, fwah-YO, which is béarnaise, the tarragon butter sauce, made richer with a reduced meat glaze. The sauce is named for the Restaurant Foyot, which stood opposite the Senate in Paris until 1937.

The guest gets the roast with its squash and a sauce rich enough to match it; whether it is carved at the table or in the kitchen is confirmed at lineup. It tastes very tender and buttery, with a savory, rich sauce.

A side of Maggie's Mushrooms or the Shells & Cheese makes it a full feast for two. With it we pour the 2010 Inglenook Rubicon by the glass, a Napa legend whose sixteen years have made it silky.

value.a:
The Redfish Véronique is a dinner entrée at $36, and the third course of our $80 dinner tasting.

Véronique, vay-ro-NEEK, is the French classic of fish with grapes. We make it with Louisiana redfish, a firm, mild Gulf fish that cooks up flaky. The grapes are pickled with hibiscus, so they are sweet, tart and floral. Braised leeks are soft and gently sweet, fingerling potatoes make it satisfying, and a beurre blanc, burr BLAHN, a silky butter sauce made with white wine, gets its brightness from preserved lemon.

The guest gets the fish over leeks and potatoes, the pickled grapes around it and the butter sauce. It tastes buttery and flaky, with sweet-tart grapes and bright lemon.

It is elegant and balanced, a classic idea with a Louisiana fish. À la carte, the Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé by Coravin is the pour, since beurre blanc and white Burgundy are a classic. On the tasting it is paired with a light red, the Louis Jadot Beaune 1er Cru, whose red fruit loves the hibiscus grapes.

The Gulf Fish en Papillote is a dinner entrée at $38, and a lighter plate that is still full of flavor.

En papillote, ahn pah-pee-YOHT, means cooked sealed in a wrapper, classically paper; here the wrapper is a banana leaf, so the fish steams gently in its own juices and stays very moist. The fish changes with what is fresh. Inside the leaf go Louisiana crab for sweetness, tomato, Castelvetrano olives, kah-stel-veh-TRAH-noh, the bright green, mild and buttery Sicilian olives, Marcona almonds, and sorghum, a chewy ancient grain.

The guest gets the parcel itself, and inside it moist fish with the crab, olives and tomato; whether it is opened at the table is confirmed at lineup. It tastes moist and delicate, bright and Mediterranean, with nutty crunch.

The banana leaf is the house's own touch on a classic method. The Pazo das Bruxas Albariño is the pour, citrusy with a salty edge, made for seafood with olives and tomato.

The Poussin à la Moutarde is a dinner entrée at $29, where a French bistro meets a Southern kitchen, and one of the best values on the dinner menu.

Poussin, poo-SAN, à la moutarde means young chicken with mustard. Ours is a Cornish hen, brined in sweet tea, which seasons it and keeps it juicy, then fried until crisp. The classic French partner is mustard, so it comes with a mustard cream sauce, tangy and rich, with turnips and shallots for a gentle sweetness.

The guest gets a whole small bird, fried golden, with the creamy sauce and the vegetables; as a whole bird, it may have bones. It tastes crisp, juicy and savory, with a tangy, creamy sauce.

It is Southern fried chicken dressed for a French table, and comforting. The Gainey Estate Chardonnay is the pour, creamy enough for the mustard sauce and fresh enough for the fried crust, and the Pierre Sparr sparkling rosé is a co-equal, because bubbles and fried chicken are a classic.

The Blackened Tofu is a dinner entrée at $25, and the plate for a guest who wants a meatless entrée, once the kitchen has confirmed how it is made tonight.

The tofu comes from Tien Dat, a Vietnamese family co-op across the river that presses it fresh every week. We blacken it, the Louisiana technique of coating in spices and searing in a very hot pan, so it gets a dark, spiced crust. It sits over rice grits from Two Brooks Farm, a family rice farm at Sumner in the Mississippi Delta: broken grains of rice cooked creamy like grits. Preserved shiitake mushrooms, shee-TAH-keh, bring deep, savory flavor.

The guest gets the dark-crusted tofu over creamy grits with the mushrooms. It tastes spiced and crusty outside, soft inside, earthy and savory, with moderate spice.

It shows the kitchen's local sourcing. The Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir is the pour: light and silky with an earthy note that loves mushrooms, and low tannin that will not clash with the spice.

The Creole Hanger Steak is a dinner entrée at $42, bold, spiced and fun.

Hanger is a butcher's favorite cut, loose-grained and very beefy, and ours is Creekstone Farms beef seasoned with our own housemade Creole spice. Broccolini is glazed with Madeira, the fortified wine, so it is a little sweet and nutty. Persillade, pair-see-YAHD, is chopped parsley and garlic, and we add pepitas, pumpkin seeds, for crunch. Chili crisp, a crunchy chili oil, brings real heat.

The guest gets sliced steak with the glossy broccolini, the green persillade and the chili crisp over it. It tastes beefy and spiced, with crunch, heat and a sweet-savory glaze.

It is the dinner hanger, spicier than the daytime one and with no egg. The Domaine de Durban Beaumes-de-Venise Rouge is the pour: ripe and generous, with soft tannins and a peppery note that love a little spice, served cool so its alcohol does not lift the heat.

value.a:
The Housemade Pork Sausage Patty is a breakfast and lunch side at $9, and the one breakfast meat we make ourselves.

We make our own pork sausage in house and form it into a patty, the classic Southern breakfast way. A Southern breakfast sausage is traditionally fresh pork shoulder seasoned with salt, black pepper and sage, often with red pepper and a touch of brown sugar; what goes into ours, and how much heat it carries, is a question for the kitchen.

The guest gets a single browned patty beside the eggs. It tastes savory, well seasoned and satisfying.

It belongs to the breakfast Owen Brennan made the event: in a city whose restaurants served lunch and dinner, he made breakfast the reason to come, and the sides are how a guest builds that breakfast out. The Eggs Sardou and the Crab & Corn Omelette carry no meat, so the sausage is the natural add; it also sits well beside the cheddar grits, the Brabant potatoes or an egg any style.

Mention first that we make it ourselves: that is what sets it apart from the bacon.

It is bacon cut thick and cooked so it stays meaty in the middle while the edges crisp up. Thick bacon wants a low, slow render, so the fat turns glassy before the edges can burn. The menu names no brand; whether the breakfast bacon is the Nueske's the dinner succotash names is a question for the kitchen.

The guest gets a plate of thick strips, browned and crisp at the edges. It tastes smoky, salty and satisfying, with a meaty bite.

It is the natural add to an egg dish without meat, the Eggs Sardou or the Crab & Corn Omelette, and a good one to share around the table with the cheddar grits or the Brabant potatoes.

Ask every guest how crisp they like it, and check with the kitchen whether it can be adjusted before promising it. It is not the coffee-cured Canadian bacon on the Eggs Hussarde, which belongs to that dish.

The Buttermilk Biscuit is a breakfast and lunch side at $5.

A buttermilk biscuit is the Southern breakfast bread. The classic method is soft flour and cold butter or lard, buttermilk reacting with baking soda to lift the dough, a few folds for layers and a hot oven. The buttermilk makes it tender and gives it a gentle tang. How ours is made each morning is a question for the kitchen.

The guest gets a warm biscuit, golden outside, soft and layered within. It tastes tender, buttery and a little tangy.

Its real job at Brennan's is the sauce. The Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen both carry hollandaise and marchand de vin, and a biscuit finishes every last bit of both. It also rounds out a lighter plate, such as the omelette, for a hungry guest.

The menu prints the biscuit alone, so butter or jam with it is confirmed with the kitchen. Offer it as the eggs are ordered, so it lands warm with them.

value.a:
Brabant Potatoes are a breakfast and lunch side at $7, and an old New Orleans restaurant classic.

They have been in the Picayune's Creole Cook Book since the early 1900s, and they are usually said to be named for the Brabant region of Belgium and the Netherlands. Potatoes are cut into cubes and cooked until golden and crisp outside and fluffy inside, then traditionally finished with garlic butter and parsley; the kitchen confirms tonight's finish at lineup.

The guest gets a bowl of golden cubes, flecked with green. They taste crisp, fluffy, buttery and garlicky.

They are the side every egg dish wants, and the best partner for the housemade sausage or the thick-cut bacon. An egg any style with a bowl of Brabant potatoes makes a small breakfast of its own. They also appear on the children's breakfast menu, with the popcorn shrimp and the grilled cheese.

The name trips people up: the guide prints bra-BAHNT, and bra-BAHN and the local bruh-BANT are both heard, so learn the house's way at lineup.

The Succotash is a dinner side at $12, and a seasonal one.

Succotash is a Native American dish of corn and beans, some four hundred years old, that the South adopted; traditionally it is corn and lima beans. Ours is a mix of glazed summer vegetables with Nueske's bacon, a Wisconsin bacon known since 1933 for its deep applewood smoke.

The guest gets a bowl of bright, glossy vegetables with pieces of smoky bacon through them. It tastes sweet and bright from the glazed vegetables, savory and smoky from the bacon.

It is a great partner for the Roasted Chateaubriand or the Poussin à la Moutarde, and a way to bring something green and seasonal to a rich dinner.

It changes with the season: the dinner menu is a late summer one, and tonight's vegetables are confirmed at lineup. It is not a meatless side, because of the bacon, so say so when a guest asks for vegetables.

The heat is moderate, so it is worth a word to a spice-shy guest. Whether it suits a guest's diet is a kitchen question: the service note marks it as one to confirm.

The Shells & Cheese is a dinner side at $12: our grown-up mac and cheese.

Pasta shells hold the sauce in every curve, and the sauce is a fondue of Mimolette, mee-mo-LET, a bright orange French cheese from Lille, nutty and a little sweet as it ages. It is made with Abita Amber, the Louisiana lager brewed at Abita Springs since 1986, for a malty depth, and finished with Grana Padano, the hard, nutty Italian cheese, for a salty finish.

The guest gets a bowl of shells in an orange cheese sauce. It tastes rich, nutty and malty, with a salty edge.

It is the side to put beside the Roasted Chateaubriand or the Creole Hanger Steak, and a favorite with anyone who loves mac and cheese.

The beer goes into the sauce, and cooking takes most of its alcohol but not all, so a guest avoiding alcohol should hear that it is made with beer.

value.a:
South Louisiana Rice Dressing is a dinner side at $12, and the side that tastes most of a South Louisiana family table.

Rice dressing is what South Louisiana families serve at Sunday dinners and holidays. Traditionally it is rice cooked with well-seasoned ground meat, often including liver for depth, and the holy trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper. The menu prints no description of ours, so which meats go into it is confirmed at lineup.

The guest gets a warm bowl of seasoned rice. It tastes savory and hearty, a lot like dirty rice: think of it as dirty rice's Cajun cousin.

It is a great partner for the Poussin à la Moutarde or the Creole Hanger Steak, and a side that gives a visitor a taste of home cooking in Louisiana.

Made traditionally it carries meat, so it is never offered as a vegetable side.

value.a:
World Famous Bananas Foster is the dessert Brennan's gave the world, $14 at every meal, flambéed at the table, with a minimum of two people per order.

It was invented here in 1951. Owen Brennan asked for a banana dessert, and chef Paul Blangé created it; the house's own telling credits Ella Brennan with Blangé. It is named for Owen's friend Richard Foster, chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission, and New Orleans was then the main port for bananas from Central America. 2026 is its 75th year.

At the cart, butter, brown sugar and cinnamon melt into a caramel; banana liqueur goes in as our published recipe has it, then the bananas to soften; then the rum is lit. As it burns, the caramel deepens. The bananas are spooned over our housemade vanilla ice cream, then the warm sauce.

It tastes warm, caramelized and boozy-sweet over cold, creamy vanilla. It closes the Traditional Breakfast with Congregation Coffee & Chicory.

value.a:
Cherries Jubilee is our other tableside flambé, a Brennan's signature at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

It is older than Bananas Foster: Escoffier made it for Queen Victoria's jubilee in the 1890s. Fresh, tart black cherries go into a warm Luxardo sauce. Luxardo, loo-KSAR-doh, is the Italian family house famous for maraschino cherries and the liqueur, founded in 1821 and making it at Torreglia, near Padua, since 1947.

At the table the sauce is lit, and as the flame burns the sauce deepens and the cherries soften. Then it all goes over our housemade vanilla ice cream, warm and cold together.

It tastes warm and tart-sweet, the cherries bright against the cold vanilla, fruitier and lighter than the Foster's caramel.

It is the flambé for a guest who is not in the mood for bananas, or the second flambé for a table that wants both. Banyuls, a sweet red from the south of France tasting of fig, caramel and cocoa, is the pour once the sommelier confirms it is poured à la carte.

The New Orleans Bread Pudding is a dessert at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: New Orleans' comfort dessert, done our way.

Bread pudding began as an old European thrift dish for stale bread and became a New Orleans staple; the Picayune's Creole Cook Book of 1901 already prints one. It is bread soaked in a sweet custard and baked until soft inside and golden on top. The warm whiskey sauce became a New Orleans restaurant signature in the 20th century; ours goes a step further with a whiskey caramel, rich and a little boozy, buttermilk ice cream with a gentle tang, and pralines, PRAH-leens, the New Orleans candy of pecans, butter and brown sugar, for crunch.

The guest gets the warm pudding with the caramel, a scoop of ice cream and the crumbled pralines. It tastes warm, soft and custardy, sweet and tangy, warm and cold.

The Dr. Hermann Auslese, honeyed with lively acidity, is the pour; the Banyuls may lead once a manager confirms it is poured outside the tasting.

The Snickers is our grown-up candy bar, $15 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and the dessert that closes the dinner tasting.

You can guess the inspiration. Each part of the candy bar becomes its own element: a milk chocolate Bavarian, a light, set cream somewhere between a mousse and a custard; a silky caramel custard; nougat turned into ice cream; and roasted peanuts for salt and crunch.

The guest gets a plated dessert with all the flavors they know, laid out as separate pieces. It tastes creamy, chocolatey and caramel-sweet, with salty, crunchy peanut.

It is nostalgic and fun, but refined. On the dinner tasting it is poured with a 4 oz glass of Banyuls, a sweet fortified red from the south of France, whose cocoa and coffee notes are chocolate's best friend and whose sweetness keeps the chocolate from turning the wine bitter. The tasting pour is the guide's Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva, confirmed at lineup.

The Lemon Tart is a dessert at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and the lightest dessert on the menu.

It has everything a lemon meringue tart has, built in layers. A yuzu mousse, YOO-zoo, is the heart of it: yuzu is a fragrant Japanese citrus that tastes like lemon, lime and mandarin at once. With it come a lemon jelly, a sweet pastry crumb for crunch, and toasted meringue, soft and marshmallowy.

The guest gets the layers of pale mousse and bright jelly over the crumb, with the browned meringue on top. It tastes bright, tart and airy, with sweet crunch.

It is the dessert to suggest after a rich meal, when a guest wants something refreshing rather than heavy. Citrus desserts are hard on wine, but a sweet Mosel Riesling loves them: the Dr. Hermann Auslese has the acidity to match the lemon, which is why it is the match, as a half-bottle, and why Banyuls is not.

The Pineapple Tarte Tatin is a dessert at $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: tropical, buttery and bright.

Tarte Tatin, tart tah-TAN, is the famous French upside-down tart, usually apples caramelized in butter and sugar on crisp pastry. We make it with pineapple, charred so it is caramelized with a little smoky edge, on puff pastry for flaky layers. The anglaise, a pourable vanilla custard, is made with sweetened condensed milk for a rich, caramel-milk flavor, and a whipped vanilla mousse keeps it light.

The guest gets the caramelized pineapple on its pastry, with the custard sauce and the mousse. It tastes caramelized, tangy and flaky, with creamy vanilla.

It is a French classic with a tropical twist, and a lighter alternative to the flambés. The Dr. Hermann Auslese is the pour: it carries pineapple and honey notes of its own, so the wine mirrors the tart, and it stays bright enough to cut the pastry and the custard.

Crawfish Meat Pies are the most Louisiana snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list, $16, served in the Roost Bar and the courtyard.

Meat pies are a Louisiana tradition: savory hand pies. At Bubbles ours are filled with crawfish and served with a chive rémoulade, ray-moo-LAHD, a tangy, herby sauce for dipping. How the kitchen makes the pastry and the filling is not printed and is a kitchen question.

The guest gets the pies with the green-flecked rémoulade beside them. They taste of savory crawfish in pastry, then the cool, bright, tangy dip.

They are the snack to suggest to a visitor who wants a local taste in the courtyard, and to share over a glass of bubbles: the Pierre Sparr sparkling rosé or the house Champagne both cut the pastry, because bubbles and acid love anything fried or baked and rich.

Bubbles runs on weekday afternoons, with the hours confirmed on shift.

They belong to the Bubbles snack list, offered on weekday afternoons; the hours are confirmed on shift.

Popcorn Shrimp are the seafood snack on the Bubbles at Brennan's list, $15, served in the Roost Bar and the courtyard.

They are bite-size fried Louisiana shrimp, crunchy and golden outside, sweet inside, and the current menu prints a Crystal gastrique with them. A gastrique is a sweet and sour sauce of caramelized sugar and vinegar; ours is made with Crystal, the New Orleans hot sauce, so it is tangy with a gentle heat. The guest gets a plate of small golden shrimp to share. They taste crunchy and sweet, the shrimp tender under the crust, with a tangy kick from the gastrique.

value.a:
The Brandy Milk Punch is a Brennan's signature drink, $12 at breakfast and lunch, and the eye opener that begins the Traditional Breakfast.

In New Orleans a proper breakfast starts with an eye opener, and the milk punch is the classic. The menu prints four things: brandy, heavy cream, vanilla bean and nutmeg. The bar shakes the brandy with the cream and real vanilla bean, serves it cold, and finishes it with nutmeg on top. No house recipe is published, so the server quotes those four and no measures.

The guest gets a cold, pale, creamy drink with the nutmeg dusted over it. It tastes creamy, smooth and a little sweet, gently boozy: think of a lighter, boozier eggnog without the egg.

It is the first sale of the morning, offered at the greeting, and the opening course of the $80 tasting, before the baked apple. For a guest who skips it, the Café Glacé de la Maison takes its place without alcohol.

value.a:
The Classic Sazerac is a Brennan's signature drink, $13 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and New Orleans' own cocktail.

The Louisiana Legislature named it the official cocktail of New Orleans in 2008: the city's, not the state's. Ours is Sazerac rye whiskey stirred with Peychaud's, PAY-shoze, the bright red New Orleans bitters with anise and cherry notes, and served without ice in a glass rinsed with Herbsaint, ERB-sant, the anise liqueur created in New Orleans in 1934. The rinse gives its aroma without much of its flavor. Sugar and lemon peel are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a short, amber, iceless drink with an anise perfume. It tastes spirit-forward, spicy and aromatic, and strong.

It is the first rung of the house's Sazerac ladder: $13, then Thompson's Dream at $20 with Willett rye, then Origin Story at $40 with Cognac and absinthe, the way the first Sazeracs were made. It suits the guest before dinner or with the steak.

value.a:
Brennan's Irish Coffee is a signature drink, $12 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: an Irish coffee with a New Orleans accent.

It starts with our dark roast coffee with chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, roasted chicory root blended in the New Orleans way, which adds a roasty, almost chocolatey depth. It is sweetened with brown sugar, spiked with Tullamore D.E.W. Irish whiskey, whose initials are those of Daniel E. Williams, the distillery's manager who became its owner, and topped with whipped cream.

The guest gets a warm coffee under a cool white cap of cream, and sips the hot coffee through it. It tastes warm, sweet and smooth, roasty from the chicory.

It is the dessert upsell, on the breakfast and lunch menu and on the dessert menu: the natural partner for Bananas Foster or the bread pudding. For a guest who wants coffee without whiskey, our New Orleans-style coffee with chicory is the same roast on its own.

value.a:
The Dulce de Leche is a signature dessert cocktail, $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: Bananas Foster in a glass.

It is made with Brennan's Blender's Reserve Don Q rum, Don Q being the Puerto Rican rum house, with crème de cacao for chocolate, cream, and a banana rum butter sauce: buttery, caramel and banana, the flavors of the Foster. Don Q's Blender's Reserve is a blend of aged rums, and Don Q sells restaurant named private casks of it; whether ours is a cask selected for Brennan's is a lineup question, so a server says only what the menu prints until the beverage team confirms the story.

The guest gets a creamy, pale caramel drink. It tastes rich and sweet: buttery caramel, banana and chocolate.

It is the drink for the guest who loves the Foster, or for dessert on its own, and the way a guest dining alone gets the Foster's flavors without the two-person minimum.

The Catalina Island is our spirit-free highball, $15 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, listed under a Temperance heading on the cocktails page.

It is built long on Seedlip Grove 42, SEED-lip, a British non-alcoholic spirit distilled on citrus, at 0.0 percent alcohol, with fresh local watermelon and tonic. The menu prints those three parts and no measures.

The guest gets a tall, bright, bubbly drink. The tonic gives it bubbles and a gentle bitterness, the watermelon a little sweetness, so it tastes bright, dry and grown-up rather than sugary.

Because it has bubbles and lift, it does at the table what Champagne does, which is why the guide makes it the zero-proof pick with thirteen dishes, from the Grand Isle Jewel oysters, the Creole Caesar and the Eggs Hussarde to the duck, the redfish and the lemon and pineapple desserts. It is the drink to offer a guest who skips the flambé or the milk punch.

value.a:
The Black Hills is our spirit-free take on a margarita, $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, listed under the Temperance heading beside the Catalina Island.

It is built on Lyre's, LY-erz, an Australian non-alcoholic agave spirit, shaken with a fresh basil purée and lime. Lyre's is labeled under 0.5 percent alcohol, so the honest word is non-alcoholic, not zero. The menu prints the three parts and no measures; whether the bar uses the Blanco or the Reserva is a lineup question.

The guest gets a green, bright drink. It tastes green, herbal and sharp, with a little earthiness from the agave.

That acidity is why it works with rich food: it cuts butter, cream and spice the way a crisp white wine would, which is why the guide makes it the zero-proof pick with thirteen dishes, from the gumbo, the crab claws and the Eggs Sardou to the steaks, the Chateaubriand and the Blackened Tofu.

value.a:
The Yellowstone is on our current cocktail list, themed Summer Vacations of 1946, the year Brennan's opened, at $18.00, the top of that list.

It is the national park trip. Uncle Nearest 1884, UN-kul NEER-ist, a small batch whiskey, is balanced with fresh lemon, a honey and turmeric syrup made in house, and Peychaud's Aperitivo, a bittersweet red aperitif under the same New Orleans name as our Sazerac bitters. The page prints those four parts; measures, method, glass and garnish are not printed.

The guest gets a golden whiskey drink. It tastes honeyed and bright, with a bittersweet aperitivo edge over the whiskey and a warm note of turmeric.

Honey and lemon make it easy to drink, and the aperitivo gives it a grown-up edge, so it is the drink for a whiskey sour lover, or for a guest who wants something lighter than a Sazerac. A fall list was expected, so a server says our current list, never our summer list.

The Miami Beach is the lightest drink on our current list, Summer Vacations of 1946, at $14.00, the lowest price on that list.

It is the beach stop. Sparkling wine is lengthened with local watermelon juice and fresh citrus. The page prints those three parts; which sparkling wine, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a pink, fizzy glass. It tastes light, fizzy and fruity, watermelon brightened by citrus, gentler than a spirit cocktail.

It is the easy yes at brunch and in the courtyard, and the sparkling twin of the Catalina Island, which carries the same watermelon without alcohol. It suits a guest who wants a drink but not a strong one, and it sits well with salty, fried snacks like the fries with pink sauce at Bubbles.

For a guest who wants to go grander after the meal, the Roost Bar pours the Flamingo, made with Taittinger Champagne, but only there, so it is an invitation to the Roost Bar, never a dining room upsell.

The Niagara Falls is the gin drink on our current list, Summer Vacations of 1946, at $15.00.

It is gin with Lillet Blanc, lee-LAY BLAHN, a light French aperitif wine, floral and citrusy, then tomato water, the clear juice of ripe tomatoes, and fresh lemon. The page prints those four parts; which gin, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a clear, pale drink. It tastes crisp and savory rather than sweet, like the freshest part of a ripe tomato, with a gentle floral, citrusy lift from the Lillet.

It is the savory drink on the list: lovely before a meal, and with the oysters or the Creole Tomato Tostada, and the one to offer a guest who likes a martini but wants something lighter.

After the meal, the Roost Bar pours the Spoonbill, the grand gin drink, but only there, so it is an invitation to the bar, never an upsell at the table.

The Havana is the island stop on our current list, Summer Vacations of 1946, at $17.00.

It is built on Appleton Estate 12 Year Old, AP-ul-tun, an aged rum rich with brown sugar and oak, with more brown sugar syrup, fresh lime and spicy ginger beer, so it drinks like a richer rum and ginger. Sfumato Rabarbaro, sfoo-MAH-toh rah-BAR-bah-roh, an Italian rhubarb amaro with a smoky edge, adds depth and a bittersweet finish. The page prints those five parts; measures, glass and garnish are confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a tall amber drink. It tastes of rich aged rum and brown sugar, ginger spice and lime, with a smoky bittersweet edge.

It is the brown spirit drink that still refreshes: for the rum and ginger drinker, for anyone who likes a dark and stormy, and as the next round after a Sazerac on a warm day. At the Roost Bar it also suits the Roost Burger.

The Acapulco is the Pacific beach on our current list, Summer Vacations of 1946, at $16.00.

It is Milagro Silver, mee-LAH-groh, an unaged tequila, clean and bright, with mezcal, mez-KAL, tequila's smoky agave cousin, and a fresh purée of melon and basil. The page prints those three parts; which mezcal, the measures, the glass and the garnish are confirmed with the bar.

It is bright and easy to drink, the one for a tequila or margarita lover. It is also the spirited twin of the Black Hills, which shares its agave and basil without the alcohol, so a table split between drinkers and non-drinkers can order the pair.

The Flamingo is one of the three luxury cocktails poured only in the Roost Bar and Lounge, at $28.00, and the Roost's celebration drink.

Thompson's Dream is the middle rung of our Sazerac ladder, $20 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: our Sazerac stepped up.

The guide prints it inside the Classic Sazerac's service note with its build and price. It is Willett 4-year rye, WILL-it, from a family distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, founded in 1936, which runs spicier and stronger than the classic's rye; Bitter Truth Creole Bitters, made in Munich as a tribute to the New Orleans style; and a glass rinsed with St. George absinthe, the first American absinthe made legally after the old ban. No measures, glass or garnish are printed; the build follows the Classic, confirmed with the bar.

The guest gets a short, iceless, amber drink like the Classic, with a greener perfume. It tastes of louder rye spice and more heat, with a more herbal rinse.

The name is the house's own; no Willett bottling carries it, so a server says it is probably named for Thompson Willett, the distillery's founder. It is the drink to offer whenever a guest orders a second Sazerac.

Origin Story is the top of our Sazerac ladder, $40 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, the highest cocktail price the guide prints.

It is the Sazerac the way it began. The first Sazeracs were Cognac and Peychaud's; rye took over once phylloxera made Cognac scarce in the 1870s and 1880s. So it is built on Dudognon, doo-doh-NYOHN, a family Cognac estate in Grande Champagne, Cognac's first growth, with Peychaud's bitters rested in a barrel and Jade Nouvelle-Orléans absinthe, created by a New Orleans native as a tribute to the city's old absinthe houses. Which Dudognon, and who ages the bitters, are lineup questions.

The guest gets a short, iceless, deep amber drink. It tastes rounder than the Classic: grape, dried fruit and oak, a softer bitters note and a floral wormwood aroma.

It is the drink for the Chateaubriand table, for a guest celebrating, and for the curious drinker who wants to taste where the Sazerac started.

Our New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory is $11 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, priced in the guide's eye openers and coffee list, where one $11 stands before all three coffees.

New Orleans coffee means coffee with chicory. Chicory, CHICK-uh-ree, is a roasted root; the city's habit is usually traced to Civil War blockade shortages, and it stuck because it adds body and a cocoa-like bitterness without any caffeine of its own. The breakfast tasting pours Brennan's private blend from Congregation Coffee, a roaster in Algiers Point, across the river.

The guest gets a hot, dark cup, served the way they take it. It tastes dark, roasty and smooth, with a gentle bitterness.

That bitterness is exactly what balances dessert, which is why the guide makes it the zero-proof pick with six sweet plates: the Framboise French Toast, the coffee cake, Bananas Foster, Cherries Jubilee, the bread pudding and The Snickers. It closes the Traditional Breakfast beside the Foster.

value.a:
The Café Glacé de la Maison is our house iced coffee, $11 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, priced and built in the guide's eye openers and coffee list.

Café glacé, ka-FAY gla-SAY, is French for iced coffee. Ours starts with chicory cold brew, so it is smooth and roasty, sweetened with a syrup of cardamom and clove, the clove a nod to the city's flamed café brûlot, and topped with an orange flower foam.

The guest gets a cold coffee under a pale, fragrant foam. It tastes cold, roasty and lightly sweet, with warm spice and a floral orange lift.

It is the guide's zero-proof pick with the baked apple, the turtle soup and the duck confit waffle, and the cold choice with the coffee cake. It is also the drink for anyone skipping the milk punch at breakfast, and a refreshing, spirit-free choice on a warm courtyard day.

value.a:
Brennan's Essential by Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut is our house Champagne, poured by the glass at breakfast and lunch and at dinner: $28 a glass on the Binwise list and $30 on the current menu, so the price is confirmed at lineup.

It is a Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut labeled for us, a blend of all three Champagne grapes, Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay, made by the traditional method. Extra Brut means very little added sugar, under six grams a liter, so it is drier than a standard Brut. Piper-Heidsieck spells its own cuvée Essentiel; the dosage and lees age wait on the sommelier confirming which cuvée is in the bottle.

In the glass it is pale and lively, with fine bubbles. It tastes very dry and crisp: citrus, orchard fruit and a little brioche, with a firm, chalky finish.

That dryness and those fine bubbles cut through rich, salty food, which is why it is the first pick with the turtle soup, the Grand Isle Jewel oysters and the Eggs Hussarde, and the second choice with the Louisiana Oysters, the Creole Caesar and the omelette. It is the house bubbles, morning and night.

value.a:
The Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d'Alsace is our sparkling rosé by the glass, $18 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Pierre Sparr, pee-AIR SHPAR, is an Alsace house. Crémant means the wine is made the same way as Champagne, with the second fermentation in the bottle, and in Alsace a rosé crémant must be all Pinot Noir.

In the glass it is pink and lively, with a creamy mousse. It tastes dry, with strawberry and red currant.

It is Champagne's method at a friendlier price, and the red fruit is what makes it useful at the table: it is the first pick with the Steak Tartare Cannoli, where red fruit suits the raw beef and the bubbles cut the fried shell and the crème fraîche. It is also the second choice with the Eggs Sardou, the Eggs Owen and the Poussin à la Moutarde, and a natural for a brunch celebration.

For a guest who wants bubbles but something pink with the Hussarde, it is all Pinot Noir and dry, with red fruit for the marchand de vin.

value.a:
Rare Brut 2012 is our prestige vintage Champagne by the glass, $75 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, poured from a bottle kept fresh under a Coravin Sparkling stopper.

Rare began as Piper-Heidsieck's prestige cuvée and is now run as its own house, Rare Champagne; its first vintage was 1976, and only about a dozen vintages have ever been declared. It is Chardonnay-led, with Pinot Noir, from a single vintage and Grand Cru sites, with about ten years on its lees. Because the opened bottle sits under a Coravin Sparkling stopper, which re-pressurizes it, a single glass is possible.

In the glass it is golden, with a long, fine mousse. It tastes of white peach, candied citrus and toasted almond.

It is the celebration step up: from the house Champagne with the turtle soup, the oysters, the Hussarde and the omelette, and wonderful with crab claws or on its own. The Binwise list and the Birthday Bubbles page print 2012, and the current Wines by the Glass page a 2013 Millésime, so the open vintage is read at lineup.

value.a:
Charles Lafitte Brut is the pairing Champagne on both of our tasting menus, poured as a 4 oz glass; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Charles Lafitte, sharl lah-FEET, is a house with roots to 1834, now part of the Vranken-Pommery group. This is a traditional method Brut, a blend led by Pinot Noir and Meunier with Chardonnay.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes dry, with fresh citrus and apple and a light toasty note.

Its job is to wake the palate up for everything after it. On the Traditional Breakfast the guide pours it with the Eggs Hussarde, the third course; on the dinner tasting it opens the meal with the Grand Isle Jewel oysters, on the $120 wine pairing. Which Charles Lafitte cuvée is poured, and whether it can be poured à la carte, are questions for the sommelier.

The Hussarde pour is disputed: the house page has shown Brennan's Essential by Piper-Heidsieck in its place, so the breakfast pour is confirmed at lineup.

value.a:
The C.H. Berres Old Vines Riesling 2022 is our Riesling by the glass, $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, and one of the two least expensive glasses on the list.

C.H. Berres, BEH-ress, is an old Mosel family estate at Ürzig in the Middle Mosel, with roots to 1510. This is Riesling from old vines on the Mosel slate, fermented to leave a touch of sweetness: about twenty grams of sugar a liter, at only 11.5% alcohol.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes light-bodied, with green apple, peach, a slaty mineral note and racy acidity under that touch of sweetness.

That little sweetness is what cools spice, and the low alcohol keeps heat from flaring, so it is the first pick with the Seafood Gumbo and the Duck Confit Waffle, where its fruit meets the maple. It loves the chili crisp on the hanger and the ’nduja on the lobster, and it is the second choice with the baked apple, the lobster, the shrimp and grits and the tofu. Six pairings hinge on how sweet the open bottle tastes, so it is tasted at lineup.

value.a:
The Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025 is our Albariño by the glass, $16 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Pazo das Bruxas, PAH-tho dahs BROO-shas, means manor of the witches: it is the Familia Torres estate in Rías Baixas, on the Atlantic coast of Galicia in Spain. Albariño is the crisp, saline white grape of that coast, and this one is unoaked and bottled young for freshness.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes of lemon and white peach, with an almost sea-spray, saline snap, dry and fresh.

That salty freshness makes it a natural with seafood: it is the first pick with the Creole Caesar, whose dressing is made with smoked oysters, and with the Gulf Fish en Papillote, with its olives and tomato; it is the still white offered with the Grand Isle Jewel oysters. It also suits the Marcona almonds on the papillote and the popcorn shrimp at Bubbles.

Its freshness fades as it warms, so it is kept iced between pours.

value.a:
The Sauvignon Blanc by the glass is our Loire white, $14 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, one of the two least expensive glasses on the list. The current menu prints it as Famille Durand, Val de Loire, 2024; the Binwise list still prints Domaine Durand, 2025, so the label is read at lineup.

The Durand family, dur-AHN, makes it in France's Loire Valley from Sauvignon Blanc. Val de Loire names the region and no village, so it is called a Loire Sauvignon Blanc, never a Sancerre. The guide described the 2025 as fermented in steel with no oak; the sommelier confirms the 2024.

In the glass it is pale and bright. It tastes bone-dry and zippy, with grapefruit, cut grass and a flinty note.

Artichokes make most wines taste oddly sweet or metallic, but this one's sharp, herbal acidity stands up to them, which is why it is the first pick with the Eggs Sardou. It also loves tomatoes and fresh herbs, so it is the second choice with the Creole Tomato Tostada and the leaner choice with the Louisiana Crab Claws.

value.a:
The Gainey Estate Vineyards Chardonnay 2023 is our California Chardonnay by the glass, $17 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner.

Gainey, GAY-nee, is a Santa Barbara County estate that farms in both the Santa Ynez Valley and the Sta. Rita Hills, and its Chardonnays have carried either appellation, so the one on the bottle is confirmed in service. It is cool-climate Chardonnay: the ocean cools the vineyards, which keeps the acidity bright.

In the glass it is golden. It tastes of lemon curd and baked apple, with a creamy texture and bright acidity.

That pairing of creaminess and freshness makes it the first pick for butter and cream: the Louisiana Oysters in their BBQ butter sauce, the Pecan Gulf Fish and the Poussin à la Moutarde with its mustard cream. It is also worth offering with the two crab dishes, keeping the Leflaive as the step up, once the sommelier confirms it tastes fresh rather than oaky.

It is served a little warmer than the crisp whites, so the creamy texture shows.

value.a:
The Domaine Leflaive Mâcon-Verzé 2022 is our white Burgundy by the glass, $40 at breakfast and lunch and at dinner, poured by Coravin.

Domaine Leflaive, luh-FLEV, is one of Burgundy's great white-wine estates, best known for Puligny-Montrachet. This is its Chardonnay from Verzé, mah-KAWN vair-ZAY, in the Mâconnais, southern Burgundy. The Coravin is a needle through the cork: the wine is poured without the cork being pulled, which is why a single glass of a wine like this is possible.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of citrus and white flowers, with a fine, chalky texture and a gentle richness.

That balance of richness and freshness is why it is the first pick with the Crab & Corn Omelette, the Louisiana Crab Claws and the Redfish Véronique in its beurre blanc, and the still white offered with the turtle soup. It is the step up from the Gainey with the oysters, the pecan fish and the poussin, and on the lobster course.

The estate's name matters to Burgundy lovers, so the label is always presented.

The Fichet Château London Mâcon-Igé 2024 is the dinner tasting's white, a 4 oz pour with the Louisiana BBQ Lobster on the $120 wine pairing; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Domaine Fichet, fee-SHAY, is a family estate at Igé, mah-KAWN ee-ZHAY, in the Mâconnais, farmed by the Fichet brothers; it is not the Meursault Fichet. Château London is a named vineyard parcel on old limestone, with some vines over a hundred years old: no castle, and nothing to do with England. The wine is made mostly in steel with a touch of old oak.

In the glass it is pale gold. It tastes of apple and citrus, with a gentle roundness and a fresh finish.

That roundness gives it the body for lobster and butter, and the fresh finish lifts the palate after the spicy ’nduja, which is why the guide pours it on that course. The pour itself is disputed: the house page has shown a Domaine Matrot Meursault 2023 on the course, so the supplement card is read before naming a producer.
